name: evio (Go epoll/kqueue event loop; Redis clone vs real Redis)
baseline: Redis 4.0.2 (C, single-threaded ae event loop on epoll) answering PING_INLINE; the same table also holds Go net/http, fasthttp and a Go net echo server, which are Go baselines and not counted here
workload: redis-benchmark -t ping_inline -q -c 50 -n 1000000 with pipeline depth 1, 8 and 16 against the real redis-server and against the evio example Redis clone (examples/redis-server/main.go), both started with GOMAXPROCS=1 on localhost.
claimed_speedup: Requests per second, evio Redis clone vs real Redis 4.0.2 (benchmarks/out/redis{1,8,16}.txt, final redis-benchmark line): pipeline 1: 177,147.92 vs 176,991.14 (parity); pipeline 8: 1,285,347.00 vs 878,734.62 (about 1.46x, derived from page data); pipeline 16: 2,123,142.25 vs 879,507.50 (about 2.41x, derived from page data). The README itself only shows chart images and states the goal 'performs on par with Redis and Haproxy'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. Go version not recorded (2017 snapshot, plain go build in benchmarks/bench-redis.sh). The Redis 4.0.2 build and its flags are not stated; the log shows a default config with transparent-huge-pages and overcommit warnings.
hardware: EC2 c4.xlarge instance (CPU model not named in the repo), client and server on localhost over IPv4; run on 2017-11-04 per the log timestamps
tradeoffs: Not a drop-in replacement for Go net or net/http (the README says so). Handlers run inside the event-loop goroutines and must not block. Linux epoll and BSD/macOS kqueue only, with a net-package fallback elsewhere. Calling it from C++ means a separate Go process.
caveats: The two servers do different amounts of work: the evio example is a tiny Redis-protocol clone (PING, ECHO, GET, SET, DEL, FLUSHDB, QUIT, SHUTDOWN, WAKE) over a Go map with an RWMutex, with no persistence, expiry, replication, statistics or the full command table, so this is not a like-for-like win over Redis. At pipeline depth 1 both are client-bound and equal. Real Redis stays at about 878k requests per second at depth 8 and depth 16 while the clone keeps climbing, and the repo gives no explanation. Only PING_INLINE was benchmarked. One run per cell, no variance, benchmark client shares the 4-vCPU instance with the server. Redis 4.0.2 is from 2017 and the flags and compiler for it are unstated. The README gives no mechanism and no table: it shows chart PNGs, so the numbers here come from the raw benchmarks/out/*.txt files in the repo. Latest two commits are README edits (2026-05-12, 2026-05-19) and the one before is from 2022-05-14.
found_via: GitHub: grepped raw READMEs of Go event-loop frameworks (tidwall/evio, panjf2000/gnet) for libuv/Redis/C comparisons; opened tidwall/evio README, benchmarks/README.md, benchmarks/bench-redis.sh, benchmarks/out/redis1.txt, redis8.txt, redis16.txt, examples/redis-server/main.go and the commits page.

name: Redcon (Go Redis-compatible server framework; clone vs real Redis)
baseline: Redis (C, single-threaded, started as 'redis-server --port 6379 --appendonly no'; version not stated)
workload: redis-benchmark -t set,get -n 10000000 -q -P 512 -c 512 against real Redis and against the Redcon example/clone.go server (in-memory map with an RWMutex; SET, GET, SETNX, DEL, PING, PUBLISH, SUBSCRIBE), Redcon run single-threaded (GOMAXPROCS=1) and multi-threaded.
claimed_speedup: Requests per second, README table: SET 2,018,570.88 (Redcon, one thread) vs 941,265.12 (Redis) = about 2.14x (derived from page data); GET 2,403,846.25 vs 1,189,909.50 = about 2.02x (derived from page data). Multi-threaded Redcon: SET 1,944,390.38 (about 2.07x, derived) and GET 3,993,610.25 (about 3.36x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.7 (flags not stated); Redis version and build flags not stated
hardware: MacBook Pro 15-inch, 2.8 GHz Intel Core i7 (README), client and server on one laptop
tradeoffs: Go library, so a C++ project would run it as a separate server or sidecar. The clone in the benchmark has none of Redis's persistence, expiry, data structures or replication. Each connection is served by Go's net package with goroutines.
caveats: First-party README numbers from the Go 1.7 era with no Redis version, no compiler, no run count and no variance. The Redis command shown disables the append-only file but not RDB snapshots, so default 'save' rules may have forked the server during a 10M-command SET run (the README says 'no disk persistence' without showing the config); Redis was only run single-threaded. The Go clone implements a handful of commands over a bare map, so the two servers do different work per command. Client, server and OS share one laptop; 512 connections and pipeline depth 512 favour batch throughput over latency. Odd result in the README itself: multi-threaded Redcon SET is slower than single-threaded. No latency numbers. The README names no mechanism for the gap. Redis-vs-Go comparison, not a runtime-level language claim.
found_via: GitHub: grepped raw READMEs of Go server frameworks (tidwall/redcon, evio, gnet, nbio) for Redis/libuv/C++ comparisons; opened github.com/tidwall/redcon, its README benchmark section, example/clone.go and the commits page.

name: ScyllaDB Rust driver (async Tokio CQL driver vs C++ driver)
baseline: ScyllaDB C++ driver (scylladb/cpp-driver, listed as 'cpp-driver' in the chart config; the benchmark README says the old 'cpp' bar was this driver on a single thread); the repo also has a DataStax C++ driver variant
workload: 'Basic' benchmark: 1,000,000 inserts against a local ScyllaDB in Docker with up to 1024 requests in flight (concurrency = 1024), total wall time per driver.
claimed_speedup: generate_chart/config.py: 1,000,000 inserts, concurrency = 1024: scylla-rust-driver 3734 ms vs cpp-driver 5510 ms (about 1.48x less time, derived from page data); gocql 14802 ms and cdrs-tokio 17840 ms in the same file.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README or config; each driver is built inside a Docker image by build.sh (script not read)
stars_or_usage: 689 stars (scylla-rust-driver); benchmark repo cvybhu/rust-driver-benchmarks has 84 commits, last 2022-08-05
tradeoffs: Rust crate; C++ programs get it through the scylla-cpp-rust-driver bindings (ScyllaDB's C++ API over the Rust core), which the benchmark repo lists as a separate driver. Async Tokio runtime inside the driver.
caveats: Vendor (ScyllaDB) benchmark. The repo README embeds a chart image (bench10to7-inserts.svg, no readable text) and says the chart 'is pretty old', that driver names changed since, and that 'cpp' was the Scylla C++ driver on a single thread while 'cpp-multi' was the DataStax C++ driver; config.py is the chart generator's input, its title says 1,000,000 inserts while the image name suggests 10^7, so config.py may be sample data and not the published chart. No hardware, no flags, no run count, no variance. The C++ baseline in config.py is the single-thread Scylla variant; the multi-threaded DataStax number is not in the file. The scylla-rust-driver README makes no speed claim. The ScyllaDB blog post that reportedly says the Rust driver beat the C++ driver (scylladb.com, 2021-07-13) could not be opened (host unreachable); a WebSearch snippet of it and of a later ScyllaDB write-up said the Rust driver was faster in their tests but used about twice the CPU of the cassandra-cpp backend in a loopback test (snippet only, not verified). The benchmark repo has no LICENSE file at HEAD. A database driver rather than a general concurrency runtime, so the category fit is loose.
found_via: WebSearch: 'scylla-rust-driver faster than C++ driver benchmark throughput Rust driver vs cpp-driver'; opened github.com/cvybhu/rust-driver-benchmarks (README, generate_chart/config.py, commits), github.com/scylladb/scylla-rust-driver and its commits page.
